message.content:
Lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) belong to two very different mammalian orders—Carnivora for the lion and Perissodactyla for the zebra.  
Their most recent common ancestor is therefore the last common ancestor of the two entire clades, **Carnivora** and **Perissodactyla**.  

That ancestor lived roughly 60–70 million years ago during the late Paleocene–early Eocene, when the larger Laurasiatherian radiation was still taking shape. It would have been a small, probably insectivorous or omnivorous mammal that gave rise to the diverse lineages that eventually produced modern carnivores (cats, dogs, bears, etc.) and odd‑toed ungulates (horses, rhinos, tapirs, etc.). In short, the common ancestor of lions and zebras is a basal Laurasiatherian mammal from the early Eocene.

The common ancestor would be a mammal from the clade Laurasiatheria, maybe the last common ancestor of the clades that gave rise to Carnivora and Perissodactyla. That would be a mammal from the Eocene, maybe the last common ancestor of the clade that includes the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla. That ancestor would be a small, probably insectivorous or omnivorous mammal. But we can say: The last common ancestor of lions and zebras is a mammal that lived around 60-70 million years ago, belonging to the clade Laurasiatheria, likely a small, insectivorous or omnivorous animal. Or we can say: The common ancestor is the last common ancestor of the clades Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which is a member of the clade Laurasiatheria. So answer accordingly.
